On degenerate reaction-diffusion epidemic models with mass action or standard incidence mechanism

Rachidi B. Salako Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Nevada Las Vegas, Affiliation: Las Vegas, NV 89154 Affiliation: Yixiang Wu Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Middle Tennessee State University Affiliation: Murfreesboro, Tennessee 37132, USA
Abstract

In this paper, we consider reaction-diffusion epidemic models with mass action or standard incidence mechanism and study the impact of limiting population movement on disease transmissions. We set either the dispersal rate of the susceptible or infected people to zero and study the corresponding degenerate reaction-diffusion model. Our main approach to study the global dynamics of these models is to construct delicate Lyapunov functions. Our results show that the consequences of limiting the movement of susceptible or infected people depend on transmission mechanisms, model parameters, and population size.

Keywords: SIS epidemic model, reaction-diffusion, dispersal rate, Lyapunov function, global dynamics.
MSC 2010: 92D30, 37N25, 35K40, 35K57, 37L15.

1 Introduction

Various differential equation epidemic models have been proposed to study the spread of infectious diseases [4, 7, 6, 14, 41], and it has been recognized that population mobility [5, 52, 55] and the spatial heterogeneity of the environment [19, 32] are key factors in disease transmissions. In order to address these issues, many reaction-diffusion epidemic models with non-constant coefficients have been proposed and studied [2, 17, 58, 59]. Specific infectious diseases modeled by diffusive models include malaria [38, 39], rabies [23, 42], dengue fever [53], West Nile virus [27, 31], influenza [40], Covid-19 [18, 25, 51, 57], etc.

In this paper, we consider the following Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) diffusive epidemic model, which is a natural extension of the classic ordinary differential equation epidemic model by Kermack and McKendrick [24]:

{∂tS=dS​Δ​S−f⁡(x,S,I)+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂tI=dI​Δ​I+f⁡(x,S,I)−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂νS=∂νI=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω.\begin{cases}\displaystyle\partial_{t}S=d_{S}\Delta S-f(x,S,I)+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle\partial_{t}I=d_{I}\Delta I+f(x,S,I)-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \displaystyle\partial_{\nu}S=\partial_{\nu}I=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega.\end{cases} (1.1)

Here, the individuals are assumed to live in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega; S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) are the density of susceptible and infected individuals at position x∈Ωx\in\Omega and time tt, respectively; dSd_{S} and dId_{I} are the movement rates of susceptible and recovered individuals, respectively; γ\gamma is the disease recovery rate; f⁡(x,S,I)f(x,S,I) describes the interaction of susceptible and infected people; ν\nu is the unit outward normal of ∂Ω\partial\Omega and the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions mean that the individuals cannot cross the boundary.

In the pioneering work by Allen et al. [2], model (1.1) with standard incidence mechanism, f⁡(x,S,I)=β⁡(x)​S​I/(S+I)f(x,S,I)=\beta(x)SI/(S+I), has been proposed and studied (β\beta is called the disease recovery rate). In [2], the authors define a basic reproduction number ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} and show that the model has a unique endemic equilibrium (EE) (i.e. positive equilibrium) if ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1. Most importantly, they show that the disease component of the EE approaches zero as dSd_{S} approaches zero if β−γ\beta-\gamma changes sign. Biologically, assuming that the population eventually stabilizes at the EE, this result indicates that the disease can be eliminated by controlling the mobility of susceptible individuals if there are places that are of low risk (i.e. β⁡(x)<γ⁡(x)\beta(x)<\gamma(x)). In contrast if the dispersal rate of infected people is limited, [45] shows that the disease cannot be completely eliminated. In [13, 62], the authors considered model (1.1) with mass action mechanism, f⁡(x,S,I)=β⁡(x)​S​If(x,S,I)=\beta(x)SI, which is algebraically simpler but mathematically more challenging. For this model, assuming again that the population eventually stabilizes at EE solutions, it has been shown that lowering the movement of susceptible people can eliminate the disease only when the size of the population is below some critical number, solely determined by γ/β\gamma/\beta, [9, 62], while infected individuals may concentrate on certain hot spots when limiting their movement [9, 47, 62]. It is important to note that stability of the EE solutions for models with standard incidence or mass action mechanism is only known in a few cases : either the population movement rate is uniform (i.e., dS=dId_{S}=d_{I}), or the ratio β/γ\beta/\gamma is constant [13, 46]. For more related works, we refer the interested readers to [10, 11, 12, 22, 26, 28, 29, 30, 34, 35, 46, 48, 49, 50, 54, 56, 60] and the references therein.

For the corresponding ordinary differential equation epidemic model of (1.1):

{S′=−f⁡(S,I)+γ​I,I′=f⁡(S,I)−γ​I,\begin{cases}S^{\prime}=-f(S,I)+\gamma I,\\ I^{\prime}=f(S,I)-\gamma I,\end{cases}

the global dynamics is determined by the basic reproduction number, which can be interpreted as the average number of infected individuals generated by one infectious individual in an otherwise susceptible population: if it is greater than one, the solution converges to an EE and the disease persists; if it is less than one, the solution converges to a disease free equilibrium and the infected individuals go to extinction. Here, the basic reproduction number is ℛ01=N​β/γ\mathcal{R}^{1}_{0}=N\beta/\gamma if f⁡(S,I)=β​S​If(S,I)=\beta SI and ℛ02=β/γ\mathcal{R}_{0}^{2}=\beta/\gamma if f⁡(S,I)=β​S​I/(S+I)f(S,I)=\beta SI/(S+I).

In this paper, we revisit model (1.1) and study the impact of limiting population movement on disease transmissions. Different from most of the aforementioned studies, we will work on the global dynamics of the time dependent model (1.1) with either dS=0d_{S}=0 or dI=0d_{I}=0 rather than consider the asymptotic profiles of the EE as dS→0d_{S}\to 0 or dI→0d_{I}\to 0. Intuitively, if the disease evolves at a faster time scale than the control of population movement, and the population eventually stabilizes at an EE, then the asymptotic profiles of the EE solutions may reflect the effect of the control strategy. However if the control of population movement happens in a faster time scale and the solution of model (1.1) converges to that of the corresponding degenerate system as dS→0d_{S}\to 0 or dI→0d_{I}\to 0, then the global dynamics of the degenerate system will better tell the impact of the control strategies.

There are several recent efforts on degenerate reaction-diffusion population models (see [15, 16, 33, 36, 37, 43, 63] and the references cited therein). In particular, the two works [9, 33] have partial results on model (1.1) with dS=0d_{S}=0, which was interpreted as the situation of a total lock down for the susceptible population. Note that when either dS=0d_{S}=0 or dI=0d_{I}=0, system (1.1) becomes degenerate and hence there is a lack of some compactness of the solution operator, which induces many challenges in the study of the large time behavior of the solutions.

Our main approach to study the global dynamics of the degenerate system (1.1) (i.e dS=0d_{S}=0 or dI=0d_{I}=0) is to construct Lyapunov functions (except for the case dS=0d_{S}=0 in subsection 3.1) and combine these with delicate analysis. In particular, in subsection 3.2, we present a Lyapunov function that one may easily draw a false conclusion using it and the convergence result based on it is very quite unusual (see Remark 3.8 and Fig. 2). In the proof of Theorem 4.6, we construct a Lyapunov function VV that does not satisfy V˙≤0\dot{V}\leq 0 (see Eq. 4.26) but we are still able to conclude the convergence of the solution.

The rest of our paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we list the assumptions and terminology and present some useful results. In section 3, we consider the model with mass action mechanism with dS=0d_{S}=0 or dI=0d_{I}=0. In section 4, we consider the model with standard incidence mechanism. In section 5, we run some numerical simulations to illustrate the results. In section 6, we compare the results from the two different mechanisms and control strategies and discuss the implications for disease control.

The following well-known result will be used after the construction of Lyapunov functions and we provide a proof for convenience.

Lemma 2.2.

Suppose that ϕ:ℝ+→ℝ+\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is Hölder continuous and ∫0∞ϕ⁡(t)​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(t)dt<\infty. Then limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t)=0.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)≠0\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t)\neq 0. Then there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and an increasing sequence of nonnegative numbers {tk}\{t_{k}\} converging to infinity such that ϕ⁡(tk)>ϵ\phi(t_{k})>\epsilon for all k≥1k\geq 1. Restricting to a subsequence if necessary, we assume that tk+1−tk>1t_{k+1}-t_{k}>1 for each k≥1k\geq 1. Since ϕ:ℝ+→ℝ+\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is Hölder continuous, there exist α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and M>0M>0 such that |ϕ⁡(t)−ϕ⁡(s)|≤M​|t−s|α|\phi(t)-\phi(s)|\leq M|t-s|^{\alpha} for all t,s≥0t,s\geq 0. Let δ=min⁡{(ϵ2​M)1α,1}\delta=\min\{(\frac{\epsilon}{2M})^{\frac{1}{\alpha}},1\}. Then ϕ⁡(t)>ϵ/2\phi(t)>\epsilon/2 for all t∈[tk,tk+δ]t\in[t_{k},t_{k}+\delta] and k≥1k\geq 1. It follows that

∫0∞ϕ⁡(t)​𝑑t≥∑k≥1∫tktk+δϕ⁡(t)​𝑑t≥∑k≥1δ​ϵ2=∞,\int_{0}^{\infty}\phi(t)dt\geq\sum_{k\geq 1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k}+\delta}\phi(t)dt\geq\sum_{k\geq 1}\delta\frac{\epsilon}{2}=\infty,

which is a contradiction. ∎

3 Model with mass action mechanism

3.1 Limiting the movement of susceptible people

First, we consider the impact of limiting the movement of susceptible people on (1.1) with mass action mechanism, that is, the long time behavior of the following degenerate system:

{∂tS=−β⁡(x)​S​I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω¯,t>0,∂tI=dI​Δ​I+β⁡(x)​S​I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂νI=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω¯.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}S=-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\bar{\Omega},t>0,\\ \partial_{t}I=d_{I}\Delta I+\beta(x)SI-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \partial_{\nu}I=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\bar{\Omega}.\end{cases} (3.1)

The following result states that the solution of (3.1) exists and is bounded:

Proposition 3.1.

Suppose that (A1)-(A2) holds and dI>0d_{I}>0. Then (3.1) has a unique nonnegative global solution (S,I)(S,I), where

S∈C1​([0,∞),C⁡(Ω¯))andI∈C⁡([0,∞),C⁡(Ω¯))∩C1​((0,∞),Dom∞​(Δ)).S\in C^{1}([0,\infty),C(\overline{\Omega}))\quad\text{and}\quad I\in C([0,\infty),C(\overline{\Omega}))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty),{\rm Dom}_{\infty}(\Delta)).

Moreover, there exists M>0M>0 depending on (the L∞L^{\infty} norm of) initial data such that

‖S⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω),‖I⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤M,∀t≥0.\|S(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ \|I(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq M,\ \forall t\geq 0. (3.2)
Proof.

First we suppose that the solution exists on some maximal interval [0,tm​a​x)[0,t_{max}), tmax∈(0,∞]t_{\max}\in(0,\infty] and prove the boundedness of it. Let M1=max⁡{‖S0‖L∞​(Ω),rM}M_{1}=\max\{\|S_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ r_{M}\}. By the first equation of (3.1), S⁡(x,t)≤M1S(x,t)\leq M_{1} for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and 0≤t<tmax0\leq t<t_{\max}. Since ∫ΩI​𝑑x≤∫Ω(S+I)​𝑑x≤N\int_{\Omega}Idx\leq\int_{\Omega}(S+I)dx\leq N for all t∈[0,tmax)t\in[0,t_{\max}), by [1, Theorem 3.1] (or Lemma 2.3), there exists M2>0M_{2}>0 depending on ‖I0‖L∞​(Ω)\|I_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} and M1M_{1} such that ‖I⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤M2\|I(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq M_{2} for all 0≤t<tmax0\leq t<t_{\max}. This proves (3.2).

The integral form of (3.1) is

{S⁡(⋅,t)=e−a​t​S0+∫0te−a⁡(t−s)​(a​S​(⋅,s)−β​S​(⋅,s)​I​(⋅,s)+γ​I​(⋅,s))​ds,t>0,I⁡(⋅,t)=et⁡(dI​Δ−a)​I0+∫0te(t−s)​(dI​Δ−a)​(a+β​S​(⋅,s)−γ)​I​(⋅,s)​ds,t>0,\begin{cases}S(\cdot,t)=e^{-at}S_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-a(t-s)}(aS(\cdot,s)-\beta S(\cdot,s)I(\cdot,s)+\gamma I(\cdot,s))ds,&t>0,\\ I(\cdot,t)=e^{t(d_{I}\Delta-a)}I_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)(d_{I}\Delta-a)}(a+\beta S(\cdot,s)-\gamma)I(\cdot,s)ds,&t>0,\end{cases} (3.3)

where a>0a>0 is chosen to be sufficiently large. Using Banach fixed point theory, one can show that (3.3) has a unique nonnegative solution (S,I)∈[C⁡([0,T],C⁡(Ω¯))]2(S,I)\in[C([0,T],C(\overline{\Omega}))]^{2} for some T>0T>0. By the first equation of (3.3), S∈C1​([0,T],C⁡(Ω¯))S\in C^{1}([0,T],C(\overline{\Omega})). By [44, Theorem 4.3.1 and Corollary 4.3.3], I∈C⁡([0,T],C⁡(Ω¯))∩C1​((0,T],Dom∞​(Δ))I\in C([0,T],C(\overline{\Omega}))\cap C^{1}((0,T],{\rm Dom}_{\infty}(\Delta)). The a priori bound (3.2) enables us to extend the solution globally. ∎

We note that the case when the total population is small (i.e., N<∫Ωr​𝑑xN<\int_{\Omega}rdx) has been addressed in the literature:

Theorem 3.2.

[9, Theorem 2.8-(i)] Suppose that (A1)-(A2) holds and dI>0d_{I}>0. Let (S,I)(S,I) be the solution of (3.1). If N<∫Ωr​𝑑xN<\int_{\Omega}rdx, then (S⁡(x,t),I⁡(x,t))→(S∗​(x),0)(S(x,t),I(x,t))\to(S^{*}(x),0) uniformly in x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} as t→∞t\to\infty, where S∗∈C⁡(Ω¯)S^{*}\in C(\bar{\Omega}) and ∫ΩS∗​𝑑x=N\int_{\Omega}S^{*}dx=N.

We are ready to study the asymptotic behavior of the solution of (3.1).

Theorem 3.3.

Suppose that (A1)-(A2) holds and dI>0d_{I}>0. Let (S,I)(S,I) be the solution of (3.1). Then ‖S⁡(⋅,t)−S∗‖L∞​(Ω)→0\|S(\cdot,t)-S^{*}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty for some S∗∈C⁡(Ω¯)S^{*}\in C(\overline{\Omega}), and exactly one of the following two statements hold:

  1. (i)

Remark 3.6.

3.2 Limiting the movement of infected people

We consider the impact of limiting the movement of infected people on (1.1) with mass action mechanism, that is, the long time behavior of the following degenerate system:

{∂tS=dS​Δ​S−β⁡(x)​S​I+γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂tI=β⁡(x)​S​I−γ⁡(x)​I,x∈Ω¯,t>0,∂νS=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω¯.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}S=d_{S}\Delta S-\beta(x)SI+\gamma(x)I,&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \partial_{t}I=\beta(x)SI-\gamma(x)I,&x\in\bar{\Omega},t>0,\\ \partial_{\nu}S=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\ I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\bar{\Omega}.\end{cases} (3.9)

We are ready to state the main result concerning the global dynamics of (3.9). Motivated by the biological meaning and expression of ℛ01\mathcal{R}^{1}_{0}, as in [2, 62], we call H+H^{+} and H−H^{-} as the high-risk and low-risk sites, respectively, where

H+={x∈Ω¯:N|Ω|​β​(x)−γ⁡(x)>0}andH−={x∈Ω¯:N|Ω|​β​(x)−γ⁡(x)<0}.H^{+}=\left\{x\in\bar{\Omega}:\ \frac{N}{|\Omega|}\beta(x)-\gamma(x)>0\right\}\ \ \text{and}\ \ H^{-}=\left\{x\in\bar{\Omega}:\ \frac{N}{|\Omega|}\beta(x)-\gamma(x)<0\right\}.

Define r~m=infx∈{I0>0}r(x)\tilde{r}_{m}=\inf_{x\in\{I_{0}>0\}}r(x) and ℳ:={x∈{I0>0}¯:r⁡(x)=r~m}\mathcal{M}:=\{x\in\overline{\{I_{0}>0\}}\ :\ r(x)=\tilde{r}_{m}\}. Biologically, ℳ\mathcal{M} consists with all the points of the highest risk relative to I0I_{0}. We will show that the infected people will concentrate on ℳ\mathcal{M} when limiting their movement.

Theorem 3.11.

Suppose that (A1)-(A2) holds and dS>0d_{S}>0. Let (S,I)(S,I) be the solution of (3.9). Then, we have

limt→∞‖S⁡(⋅,t)−S⁡(⋅,t)¯‖Lp​(Ω)=0,∀p∈[1,∞).\lim_{t\to\infty}\|S(\cdot,t)-\overline{S(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}=0,\quad\forall\ p\in[1,\infty). (3.22)

limt→∞∥I(⋅,t)∥L∞(K∪{I0=0})=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\|I(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(K\cup\{I_{0}=0\})}=0 (3.23)

for any compact set K⊂H−K\subset H^{-} if H−H^{-} is not empty, and the following conclusions hold:

  • (i)

    If H+∩{I0>0}=∅H^{+}\cap\{I_{0}>0\}=\emptyset, then ‖S⁡(⋅,t)−N/|Ω|‖L∞​(Ω)→0\|S(\cdot,t)-N/{|\Omega|}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0 and ∫ΩI⁡(x,t)​𝑑x→0\int_{\Omega}I(x,t)dx\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty;

  • (ii)

    If H+∩{I0>0}≠∅H^{+}\cap\{I_{0}>0\}\neq\emptyset, then there is a sequence {tk}k≥1\{t_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} converging to infinity such that ‖S⁡(⋅,tk)−r~m‖L∞​(Ω)→0\|S(\cdot,t_{k})-\tilde{r}_{m}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0, ∫ΩI⁡(x,tk)​𝑑x→N−|Ω|​r~m\int_{\Omega}I(x,t_{k})dx\to N-|\Omega|\tilde{r}_{m} and I⁡(⋅,tk)→0I(\cdot,t_{k})\to 0 as k→∞k\to\infty almost everywhere on {x∈Ω:r⁡(x)≠r~m}\{x\in\Omega:\ r(x)\neq\tilde{r}_{m}\}. In particular, if ℳ={x1,⋯,xL}⊂{I0>0}\mathcal{M}=\{x_{1},\cdots,x_{L}\}\subset\{I_{0}>0\}, then I⁡(⋅,tk)→(N−|Ω|​r~m)​∑i=1Lci​δxiI(\cdot,t_{k})\to(N-|\Omega|\tilde{r}_{m})\sum_{i=1}^{L}c_{i}\delta_{x_{i}} weakly as k→∞k\to\infty, where 0≤ci≤10\leq c_{i}\leq 1, ∑i=1Lci=1\sum_{i=1}^{L}c_{i}=1, and δxi\delta_{x_{i}} is the Dirac measure centered at xix_{i}.

From this point, we shall suppose that n=1{n=1} and complete the proof of the theorem. In view of Lemma 3.10 and inequality (3.24), we have

limt→∞‖S⁡(⋅,t)−S⁡(⋅,t)¯‖W1,2​(Ω)=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}\|S(\cdot,t)-\overline{S(\cdot,t)}\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}=0.

To prove (i)-(ii), we claim that

5 Simulations

In this section, we run numerical simulations to illustrate the results. Let Ω=[0,1]\Omega=[0,1], S0=2+cos⁡(π​x)S_{0}=2+\cos(\pi x) and I0=1.5+cos⁡(π​x)I_{0}=1.5+\cos(\pi x). Then the total population is N=∫Ω(S0+I0)​𝑑x=3.5N=\int_{\Omega}(S_{0}+I_{0})dx=3.5.

5.1 Mass action mechanism

We first simulate the models with mass action mechanism.

Simulation 1: control the movement of susceptible people. Let dS=0d_{S}=0, dI=1d_{I}=1, and γ=4−π​sin⁡(π​x)\gamma=4-\pi\sin(\pi x). Firstly, choose β=0.5\beta=0.5, and so N<∫Ωγ/β​𝑑x=4N<\int_{\Omega}\gamma/\beta dx=4, i.e. the total population is small. By Theorem 3.3, we have I⁡(⋅,t)→0I(\cdot,t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty and the infected population will be eliminated, which is confirmed by Figure 1(a). Then, choose β=2\beta=2, and so N>∫Ωγ/β​𝑑x=1N>\int_{\Omega}\gamma/\beta dx=1, i.e. the total population is large. Now Corollary 3.5 predicts that S⁡(⋅,t)→γ/βS(\cdot,t)\to\gamma/\beta and I→I∗=(N−∫Ωr​𝑑x)/|Ω|=2.5I\to I^{*}={(N-\int_{\Omega}rdx)}/{|\Omega|}=2.5, which is confirmed by Figure 1(b). Finally, choose γ=0.5​(1+x)\gamma=0.5(1+x) such that ∫Ωr​𝑑x=∫Ωγ/β​𝑑x≈2.82\int_{\Omega}rdx=\int_{\Omega}\gamma/\beta dx\approx 2.82 and S0−rS_{0}-r changes sign on Ω\Omega (By Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.5, we have already known that N=∫Ωr​𝑑xN=\int_{\Omega}rdx is a threshold value for the two alternatives in Theorem 3.3 if β\beta is a constant or S0−rS_{0}-r does not change sign on Ω\Omega). Replace the initial condition by I0=a+c​o​s​(π​x)I_{0}=a+cos(\pi x) and then N=∫Ω(S0+I0)​𝑑x=a+2N=\int_{\Omega}(S_{0}+I_{0})dx=a+2. Figure 1(c) shows ∫ΩI⁡(x,40)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}I(x,40)dx as a function of NN, which indicates that a bifurcation appears at N≈2.82N\approx 2.82, i.e. N≈∫Ωr​𝑑xN\approx\int_{\Omega}rdx is a threshold value for alternative (i) vs (ii) in Theorem 3.3. It is still an open problem to rigorously show whether N=∫Ωr​𝑑xN=\int_{\Omega}rdx is the threshold value for the two alternatives in Theorem 3.3 without the additional assumptions in Corollary 3.5. From the simulations, we can see that the disease can be eliminated only when the total population is small by controlling the movement of susceptible people.

Simulation 2: control the movement of infected people. Let dS=1d_{S}=1 and dI=0d_{I}=0. Firstly, choose β=0.2\beta=0.2 and γ=4−π​sin⁡(π​x)\gamma=4-\pi\sin(\pi x) such that H+=∅H^{+}=\emptyset. By Theorem 3.11, S⁡(⋅,t)S(\cdot,t) converges to N/|Ω|=3.5N/|\Omega|=3.5 and I⁡(⋅,t)I(\cdot,t) converges to 0, which is confirmed by Figure 2(a). Then, choose β=1\beta=1 and γ=4−π​sin⁡(π​x)\gamma=4-\pi\sin(\pi x) such that H+≠∅H^{+}\neq\emptyset and the minimum of γ/β\gamma/\beta is attached at x=0.5x=0.5. By Theorem 3.11, the infected people will concentrate at x=0.5x=0.5, which is confirmed by Figure 2(b). Finally we choose β=2\beta=2 and γ=14−4​π​sin⁡(4​π​x)\gamma=14-4\pi\sin(4\pi x) such that H+≠∅H^{+}\neq\emptyset. The minimum of γ/β\gamma/\beta is attached at x=1/8,5/8x=1/8,5/8, and the infected people concentrate at these two points as shown in Figure 2(c). From the simulations, we can see that the infected people may not be eliminated by controlling the movement of infected people if H+≠∅H^{+}\neq\emptyset. Instead, the infected people will concentrate at certain points that are of the highest risk.

5.2 Standard incidence mechanism

We then simulate the models with standard incidence mechanism.

Simulation 3: control the movement of susceptible people. Let dS=0d_{S}=0 and dI=1d_{I}=1. Firstly, choose β=1+sin⁡(π​x)\beta=1+\sin(\pi x) and γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 such that ∫Ω(β−γ)​𝑑x=2/π−0.5>0\int_{\Omega}(\beta-\gamma)dx={2}/{\pi}-0.5>0, the high-risk sites are H+=(1/6,5/6)H^{+}=(1/6,5/6), the low-risk sites are H−=[0,1/6)∪(5/6,1]H^{-}=[0,1/6)\cup(5/6,1] and moderate-risk sites are H0={1/6,5/6}H^{0}=\{1/6,5/6\}. Since H−≠∅H^{-}\neq\emptyset, Theorem 4.2-(i) predicts that infected population will be eliminated and susceptible people occupy H−∪H0H^{-}\cup H^{0}. Moreover since ∫Ω(β−γ)>0\int_{\Omega}(\beta-\gamma)>0, then ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1 and Remark 4.3 suggests that the local size of the susceptible population maybe significantly low on some portion of the high-risk area, which is confirmed by Figure 3(a). Then choose β=2.5+sin⁡(π​x)\beta=2.5+\sin(\pi x) and γ=1.5+sin⁡(π​x)\gamma=1.5+\sin(\pi x) such that β>γ\beta>\gamma and I∗=N/∫Ω(β/(β−γ))​𝑑x≈1.1159I^{*}=N/\int_{\Omega}(\beta/(\beta-\gamma))dx\approx 1.1159. Theorem 4.2-(ii) predicts that I⁡(⋅,t)→I∗I(\cdot,t)\to I^{*} as t→∞t\to\infty, which is confirmed by Figure 3(b). Finally, choose β=2−sin⁡(π​x)\beta=2-\sin(\pi x) and γ=1\gamma=1 such that β≥γ\beta\geq\gamma, H0={0.5}H^{0}=\{0.5\}, and ∫Ω1/(β−γ)​𝑑x=∞\int_{\Omega}1/(\beta-\gamma)dx=\infty. As shown in Figure 4, infected people are eliminated which agrees with Theorem 4.4. Moreover, susceptible people seem to concentrate near H0H^{0}, which we cannot prove. Our theoretical results and simulations show that the disease may be controlled by limiting the movement of susceptible people if there exist low-risk or moderate-risk sites.

Simulation 4: control the movement of infected people. Let dS=1d_{S}=1 and dI=0d_{I}=0. Firstly, choose β=2−|x−0.5|0.5\beta=2-|x-0.5|^{0.5} and γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 such that the high-risk sites are H+=(0.25,0.75)H^{+}=(0.25,0.75) and ∫Ω1/|β−γ|​𝑑x<∞\int_{\Omega}1/|\beta-\gamma|dx<\infty. As shown in Figure 5(a), S⁡(⋅,t)S(\cdot,t) converges to a positive constant and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) is positive when x∈H+x\in H^{+}. Then we choose β=2−sin⁡(π​x)\beta=2-\sin(\pi x) and γ=1.5\gamma=1.5 such that the high-risk sites are H+=(0,1/6)∪(5/6,1)H^{+}=(0,1/6)\cup(5/6,1) and ∫Ω1/|β−γ|​𝑑x=∞\int_{\Omega}1/|\beta-\gamma|dx=\infty. The infected people will live in H+H^{+} as shown in Figure 5(b). From the simulations, we can see that the infected people may be eliminated exactly at the low-risk sites by controlling the movement of infected people, which is predicted by Theorem 4.6.

6 Conclusions

We studied the impact of limiting population movement on disease outbreak by examining the large time behavior of classical solutions of a class of epidemic models with mass action or standard incidence transmission mechanism. To this end, we set the diffusion rate of the population subgroups (susceptible or infected) to zero separately and presented detailed mathematical analysis of the corresponding degenerate epidemic models. First, we established the existence and uniqueness of global classical solutions (see Propositions 3.1, 3.7, 4.1 and 4.5). Next, we discussed the global dynamics of the solutions (Theorems 3.3, 3.11, 4.4, and 4.6). Finally, we conducted some numerical simulations to complement and illustrate our theoretical results (see Figures 1-5). Our results revealed the intricate effects of restricting population movement on disease dynamics and how predictions may depend on the choices of transmission mechanisms and spatially heterogeneous parameters.

First, we considered the global dynamics of the model with mass action transmission mechanism. We defined a risk function r:=γ/βr:={\gamma}/{\beta} as the ratio of the recovery and transmission rates. When the susceptible population movement is restricted, Theorem 3.3 indicates that the average population size, N/|Ω|{N}/{|\Omega|}, compared to that of the risk function, ∫Ωr​𝑑x/|Ω|\int_{\Omega}rdx/|\Omega|, largely determines the disease outcome. In particular, regardless of the magnitude of the movement rate of the infected population, the disease may be eradicated only if the average population size is smaller than the average risk function. Moreover if the disease persists, the infected population would eventually be uniformly distributed across the whole habitat. On the other hand, when the movement of the infected population is restricted, Theorem 3.11 suggests that the disease could be eradicated only if the habitat does not have a high-risk area. Moreover, whether the magnitude of the movement rate of the susceptible population affects the results depends on whether the average size of the population is larger than the risk function in at least one location. Furthermore when the disease persists, the infected population would concentrate on the highest-risk area of the habitat. Our simulations in Figures 1-2 illustrated the above theoretical results.

Next, we studied the global dynamics of the model with standard incidence mechanism. Theorems 4.2 and 4.4 indicate that restricting the susceptible population’s movement could completely eradicate the disease only if the habitat accommodates either a low-risk or moderate-risk area. These requirements are achieved if the local distribution of the risk function is less than or equal to one. However when the habitat consists of only high-risk areas, the disease would persist with the infected population being uniformly distributed across the whole habitat. On the other hand, when the movement of the infected population is restricted, Theorem 4.6 indicates that the disease may persist if the habitat has a nonempty high-risk area. Moreover, the infected population precisely occupy the high-risk sites, and the magnitude of the movement of the susceptible subgroup does not influence the disease persistence. Our simulations in Figures 3-5 illustrated these theoretical results.

Our above theoretical results suggest that the transmission mechanisms play an important role when the population movement of one subgroup is restricted. Indeed, when mass action mechanism is used, the persistence of the disease depends on the average population size compared to either the average of the risk function (when dS=0d_{S}=0) or its local distribution (when dI=0d_{I}=0). However, when standard incidence mechanism is adopted, the disease persistence prediction depends on whether the habitat has only high-risk areas (when dS=0d_{S}=0) or has a nonempty high-risk area (when dI=0d_{I}=0). Interestingly, our results suggest that for either mass action or standard incidence mechanism disease control strategies which focus on limiting the movement of the susceptible population should be preferred over those focusing on restricting the movement of the infected population.

Finally, we point out that most of the previous works (e.g., [2, 9, 13, 45, 62]) considered the asymptotic profiles of the EE solutions to understand the effects of limiting population movements on the dynamics of infectious diseases, under the assumptions that the evolution of the disease happens on a fast scale compared to control strategies and populations ultimately stabilize at the EE solutions. In this work, we study the effects of limiting population movement by focusing on the global dynamics of the degenerate systems with either dS=0d_{S}=0 or dI=0d_{I}=0, assuming instead that the control strategies happen on much faster scale than the evolution of the disease. We remark that some of our results depend on the initial value. Other than that, the biological implications from these two approaches seem to align well (e.g., both approaches predict that the effectiveness of controlling the movement of susceptible people with mass action mechanism depends on the size of the total population).
